column2: the writer's notes (doubts; where the article disagrees with the entry): for the data check
The article says his father reappeared on the royal rolls on 24 January 1247, an evident slip for 1274; left out. The article's lead names his son Álvaro (d. 1287) as first-born; not used.

The entry says he fought the British from 1891; the article dates the British declaration of war to 1 January 1894 and the war to 1894–1899. Neither start year printed; the declaration of 1894 is given as a dated fact only. Article gives exact birth date 18 June 1853; entry has c. 1853. Left out the article's unsourced-sounding claims of abolishing the slave trade and promoting human rights.
The article gives the canal both as Jaya Ganga and as Yodha Ela.
SKIPPED: article has under 300 words, nearly all of it already in the description (parentage, Cook's visit and death, succession of Kiwalao and Kamehameha)
Short article (about 380 words); text kept to its facts. The entry's dates of the 1282-1299 revolt and the 1363-1367 resistance are not in the article and are not repeated.
The article dates his rule of Herat from 1826; the entry speaks of father and son holding Herat from about 1818. Both are consistent: father held it from 1818, Kamran ruled from 1826.

The article gives his birth as 31 January 1820 in the lead but September 1819 in its Early life section; no birth date printed. The entry spells the second assassin Myingondaing; the article has Myinkhondaing. Left out the epilogue on Ne Win's marriage to his great-granddaughter and the popular belief in British plots.

The entry dates the temple's beginning to the 1440s under Arikesari Parakrama Pandya; the article's lead says Parakrama Pandyan built it in the 13th century, its History section dates his rule to 1428-1460 and also gives 1309, and cites a temple inscription of 1384 under Vira Pandyan. No founding date and no 1384 inscription printed.

The entry says more than two hundred states; the article says some 200 in its lead and 193 in its list section. No count printed. The article says eight first-class states but lists nine names; the count is left out.
Short article; the entry's mention of the 1768 rising and the Motronynskyi Monastery is not in it. The decree of 1968 is dated 1 October 1968 in the article.
SKIPPED: article has about 300 words, most of it already in the description; it also dates the site from the 6th century against the entry's 7th to 11th
The article places Kibiro on the south-eastern shore in its lead and the eastern shore in its setting section; the entry says eastern, used without a compass point.
Left out the article's ranking of the conurbation as Malaysia's fourth largest.
The article says the great-grandfather bought the house in the seventeenth century, which is hard to square with the generations; the century is left out.

The article dates the kingdom 978-1118 in its lead and has the last rulers lose Tashir between 1111 and 1113, and the Principality of Tavush lasting 1113-1145; the entry has David IV take Lori in 1118 and the family keep Tavush and Matsnaberd afterwards. No year given for the loss of Tashir or for Tavush. The article dates David Anhoghin's accession to 989 while also giving Smbat II's death as 977/989 and Gurgen's death around 998; David's accession year left out. The article's Kakheti-Hereti dates (1029/1038-1105) left out.
The article does not state the Marechaussee's own role in Van Daalen's killings or in the Koeto Reh massacre; the text gives them as part of the campaign in which the corps' tactics were used.
The article says the town almost withstood the 1807 siege; the outcome is left out. The entry's claim of one of the largest inland harbours in the region is not in the article.

The article gives a six-year reign but also reports the tradition that he died in the 9th year of his reign; the latter is left out. The chronicles disagree on his birth, death and reign dates. The entry's sack of Pinya by Shan forces in 1364 is not in the article.

SKIPPED: article has about 230 words of substance (the song's story, its wartime popularity, a 1939 performance and three films); too little for a longer text without padding The article dates the lyrics 1914; no conflict with the entry.

Article says of the Limahong attack of 1574 both that Lakandula helped repel Limahong and that he 'was able to raise a rebellion against the Spaniards'; the entry says he supported the Spanish. Left the episode out. Article says Manila 'was not conquered, but occupied through a peace pact'; the entry says Legazpi 'took Manila'. Worded neutrally. Article dates a first battle 'May 24, 1570' after the Spaniards' 1571 arrival: an internal slip; not used.
The article gives the population densities in 'people per hectare'; kept as given. Article dates are given as 500 BC and 1400 AD; written as 500 BCE and 1400.

Disagreement with the entry: the article says the site was abandoned around 750 (stated twice), the entry says it was occupied mainly 600-800 and abandoned around 800 CE. No end date given in the text. The article's 'it is believed that the Lambityeco population might have moved to the Yagul site, located a few kilometers west' - direction stated vaguely; written as 'a few kilometres away'. Etymology: the article gives two theories; used the one it calls accepted.

The article gives the king's reign (1341-1351) but not the founding year 1344 given in the entry; no conflict. Article spells the king Bhuvanekabahu IV; the entry Bhuvanaikabahu IV. Kept the article's spelling.

The article says the song was 'written by' Esparza Oteo; the entry says 'credited to'. Not repeated. The article's sentence on naming children after saints is loose and not clearly tied to the song; left out.

The article says that after 1827 the holder 'no longer had either political or spiritual power'; the entry says he 'lived on with sacred rank but little power'. Worded as 'little real power' to avoid a contradiction. Short article (about 260 words); text kept near the lower limit.
The article counts three rebellions, 1465, 1467 and 1468; the entry's dates 1465-1468 agree.
No conflicts with the entry's dates (tune 1686, words 1686, broadsides 1688).

The article dates Constantius II's battle with the Limigantes to 357 and their breach of the treaty to 358; the entry dates his campaign to 358-359. Years left out of the text. The article says the expelled Arcaragantes settled 'in the area of the Victohali, to the south of the Danube'; the entry says many refugees were settled in the Roman Empire by Constantine. Left out where they settled. The article spells the masters Agaragantes, Arcaragantes and Argaragantes (entry); used the article's spellings where it gives them.

The article dates the Pequot War 1636-37; the entry 1636-1638. Years left out. The article says he was hired by the Connecticut Company for the Connecticut Colony; the entry says for the Saybrook Colony. Colony not named in the text. The last sentence follows the lead ('held by his descendants'); the descendants list ends with the current owner, Alexandra Creel Goelet.
The article dates the ban on other parties to 1936 ('ahead of the June 1936 election'); the entry says 'from the mid-1930s'. Consistent.

The article gives his death as 16 February 914 and says the capture came after the city fell in winter 913, without dating the capture; the entry says he was captured in 913. Capture left undated. The entry says he 'imprisoned' his father; the article says house arrest. Consistent in substance.

SKIPPED: article has about 250 words and adds little to the entry The article contradicts itself on Elen: its lead says Hywel Dda 'was married to Llywarch's daughter Elen', later it calls this a 'supposed marriage' of later Welsh tradition and says Hywel took Dyfed by force after the brief rule of Llywarch's brother Rhodri ap Hyfaidd. The entry states the marriage as fact and says Hywel then took over Dyfed: worth a second source.
The 'Death and legacy' section tells only his death; the article says nothing more about his legacy.

The article dates her regency 1324-1331 (from her father-in-law's death); the entry says she governed as regent 'after her husband's death in 1323'. Text gives the father-in-law's death without dating the regency's start. The article uses 'armistice'; written as 'truce'.

The article's account of the three Free State-Basotho wars is garbled ('Seqiti War which included two conflicts in 1856 to 1866'); left out. The heart-eating story is told as reported, as the article does. Spellings kept as the article gives them: Graaf-Reinet (usually Graaff-Reinet), Moordernaarspoort, Jammersbergspuit (usually Jammersbergspruit), Lautre.

SKIPPED: article has under 300 words and disagrees with the entry on its central points The article says Bych was the first Chairman of the Kuban Rada / head of the Kuban People's Republic from November 1917 to March 1918; the entry says he led its government in 1918-1919 and headed the delegation to the Paris Peace Conference in 1919, which the article does not mention. The article gives his death as 12 January 1945 in the lead and 12 January 1944 in the text; the entry has 1945. The article adds that he was Mayor of Baku 1912-1917 and taught at the Ukrainian Economic Academy in Poděbrady from 1922.

The article is uneven and partly hagiographic: it claims Luo's army 'defeated the Dutch army twice', quotes The Times of 8 June 1793 in an implausible translation, and gives inconsistent ages (failed the examination 'at 35' in 1772 though born 1738; died 'at the age of 58'). All left out. The article dates the Grand General System to 1777 and quotes Abdurrahman Wahid giving 1776; the entry's 1777 kept, 1776 not used. Birthplace is given variously as Sak-san-po, Meixian Shifan Town and Shishan; text says only Jiaying Prefecture (now Meixian District).
The article spells talukdars as thalukdars; written in the common form talukdars. The entry says most states paid tribute to Baroda; the article says several did, so no proportion is given.

The article gives his birth as 1675 or 1680 (many sources 1675, others nearer 1680); the entry's 1675 is not contradicted, but the birth year is left out. The entry says Megat Sri Rama murdered him because the sultan had his pregnant wife killed. The article says European and local texts report that various officials stabbed him, and treats the Megat Sri Rama story as the most popular of the legends that arose to reduce the elite's complicity. Who struck the blow is therefore left out of the text. The article also differs on where he was killed (on the way to the royal mosque or in the market); left out.
The article's present-day traffic figures (250 trains a day in each direction, 600 on the bridge) and its forecast of a high-speed line to be built 2011-2017 are left out.

The article gives several start dates (lead: around the middle of the 18th century; Macknight: about 1720, earliest recorded voyage 1751; others c. 1640 or earlier from rock art). The entry follows the mid-18th-century date; the start is not discussed in the text. The article contradicts itself on the last Makassan: Using Daeng Rangka is called the last trepanger to visit Australia, but Mangnellai Daeng Maro is called the last Makassan known to have made contact (d. 1978). The text only says Rangka's perahu was the last to leave in 1907.
The article's lead places his suicide near Osaka; its body says Mount Tennozan, as the entry does. Only Mount Tennozan is used.

The article says Mamia left a two-year-old son David, but gives David's birth as 1818 (eight years old in 1826); David's age is left out. The entry dates his rule from 1797 (when Kaikhosro proclaimed him ruler); the article dates it from 1809 (when he took power). The text tells both events without calling either the start of his reign.
The article dates the Battle of Lake Regillus to 498 BC; the entry says around 496 BCE. The battle is mentioned without a year.
The article says nothing of the popular movement against the monarchy or of the merger into Uttar Pradesh that the entry mentions; those points are not repeated.

The article contradicts itself on when V. P. Singh moved to implement the report (1989 in the Protest section; 7 August 1990 elsewhere, as in the entry); 1990 is used. The article's present-day creamy-layer limit (8 lakh rupees) is left out.

The entry says the manifesto was presented to the French authorities in February 1943; the article says it was published on 10 February 1943 but handed to the governor-general on 31 March 1943, with the addendum in May. The 31 March date is left out. The article names the governor-general 'Marchen Peyrouton' (probably a slip for Marcel); only the surname is used.

The entry says he held Molina under Castilian overlordship; the article calls his rule there semi-independent and says he styled himself count by the grace of God, implying his power did not come from the king. The question of his standing at Molina is left out.
SKIPPED: The article is about the Manyema people, a Bantu ethnic group, not the region of the eastern Congo that the entry describes.
SKIPPED: The article is about the hereditary title and its ten holders, not the statesman Sebastiao Jose de Carvalho e Melo whom the entry describes; it holds almost nothing on his career.
The article does not mention his office as Rajpramukh beyond the lead; not repeated. The 2013 lawsuit by his son over the sale of Rewa Kothi in Mumbai is left out (it concerns a living person).

SKIPPED: The article has under 250 words of substance (location, the dimensions of the earthwork, the move to Welshpool and the siege of 1212); it also dates the destruction to 1213 in its lead and to 1212 in its body, as the entry does.

The article names Isa Kotaku (1684-1745) as his tea mentor, but Kotaku died six years before Harusato was born; the text says only that Harusato's tradition descended through Kotaku. The article's Death section is empty. The entry's ginseng production, school of tea and collection of utensils are not in the article and are not repeated.

The article says he was born on a British ship en route to Mauritius; the entry calls him English-born. Birthplace left out. The article calls him Chief Justice from 1858; the entry calls him the first judge from 1858 and chief justice from 1870. Titles before 1870 kept general.
The entry says he served Henry II; the article does not mention Henry II, so the point is not developed. The historian Curtis is named only by surname in the source.
The source leaves the year of Ardashir's conquest blank; the entry's 'around 222 CE' is not repeated. Mihr-shah is spelt Mihr-šāh in the source; written without diacritics.

The source dates his capture under a flag of truce to December 1838; the entry says he was captured in 1837. The year is left out. The source writes 'Charlestown, South Carolina'; the town is left unnamed. It also gives his death as December 1848 or January 1849 in the lead, 2 January 1849 later.
The entry's point on the Ram Khamhaeng inscription is not in the source and is not repeated.

The source calls him a secular priest and also says he entered the Augustinian order; neither is stated. Birth: 'perhaps either 1530 or 1535'; the entry says c. 1535. Year left out. The source says he finished the Miscelánea in 1586 at Lima 'where he resided from 1596 to 1604', which does not agree with itself; no Lima dates given.

The source calls Khayi both his younger brother (lead) and his younger half-brother; half-brother used. Some chronicles, such as the Inzauk Razawin, date the second invasion to 1430; the entry and the main account give 1429.
SKIPPED: article too thin: about 280 words, mostly his election in 1673; it also says Siam attacked Burma in his reign, against the entry's period of peace on the frontiers
SKIPPED: article too thin: under 250 words of substance beyond the description (a family list); it dates his kingdom to 1465, the middle of the century, against the entry's late 15th century
SKIPPED: article too thin: about 230 words of history and architecture; it calls the house the richest foundation of the county of Urgell, the entry of Pallars

The source says Nanny 'founded' the community and also that Moore Town was founded in 1740 as New Nanny Town; written as the settlement of her people after the treaty. The entry's mention of Nanny's grave is not in the source. Present-day colonel and 2009 population left out.
The source dates the statue to the 470s BCE; the entry gives about 470 to 450 BCE. No date range stated, only the evidence.

The source's founding date of 28 March 1028 and its king list with exact years for the early kings are legendary or unsourced; left out. The source names 'Chief Sigcawu' as king in 1959 although its own list has Sigcawu dying in 1905; left out. The source has no account of the annexation of 1894 given in the entry; nothing on it is added. Supernatural details of the Zulu wars left out.
Abu'l-Faraj dates his death to August 900; the main date in the source is 3 October 900, which agrees with the entry.
The source gives his reign as 1470 to 1475 without 'c.'; consistent with the entry.
The source traces the lineage from the early historic period; the entry speaks of the early medieval period. Both periods are covered without a start date.

The source describes a political crisis and civil war that, with low Nile floods, produced the famine; the entry puts the cause in the floods alone. Both are stated without making either the sole cause. The source says most of Fustat's people died; the entry says Cairo's population was halved. Fustat's losses are not given.

The source dates the Battle of Tellaru to 830 but his reign to 846–869, which does not agree; no year given for the battle. The entry's Takua Pa inscription is not in the source, which speaks only of a Vishnu temple in Siam.
The source's date for her, c. 1300 BCE, is left out; the entry has 14th century BCE.
The lead dates the Toungoo revolt 1451-1459, the section 1452 (assassination of Minkhaung I) to 1459; the text gives only 1459. Chronicle troop numbers left out as exaggerated.

The entry says Persian inscriptions; the article calls the Mahakali Gate's inscriptions Arabic (with a Quranic verse). Language left unstated. Much of the article reflects a local family's claims (Rana Killedar family, Hindu origin of the buildings); left out as tradition without clear sourcing. The gate's inscription is dated 1486, the fort's capture by Fathullah 1487, as the article gives them.

The article says he seized Edessa from the Romans in 1026 (the Byzantines); the entry says he kept peace with the Byzantine Empire, which holds for most of the reign. The article does not say Mumahhid al-Dawla was his brother, so it is not stated.
The article names Lomvula Mndzebele both as Ndvungunye's mother and as the queen regent before Sobhuza's accession; both kept as given.

Birth order is disputed: the Đại Nam chính biên liệt truyện lists him as the middle brother (Nhạc, Lữ, Huệ), other sources as the youngest, as the entry has it. Left out of the text. The article gives no birth year; the entry's 1754 is not in it.

The article does not mention the Keate Award or his accepting British protection; it says the diggers' republic was annexed as Griqualand West. Diamonds are dated only to the 1860s (the entry: late 1860s), so no decade is given.

The article's Contents section is a garbled machine translation; only the plainly stated points are used (ten categories, rice methods, ploughing, sowing, manures, later additions). The named crops of the ten categories are given only in hanja and are not spelled out.

The article gives the X class as introduced at the opening in 1909 in one place and as used on the central section from 1908 in another; no year is given for it. Present-day journey times and rolling stock lists left out.

The entry calls him the legendary founder; the article's main account makes his grandfather Olu Iwa the first Awujale, while two regnal lists make Obanta the first. Both are given as accounts, without calling either the founder.
The article does not give Kishi's first name; only the surname is used. The 40th-anniversary paragraph (dated 2011 in the article) and the 'as of 2017' remarks left out.

The article dates the national union to 1695; the entry dates the founding of the empire to around 1700, so no year is given for the union. The Seventy-Seven Laws and the Golden Stool are in the entry and not repeated.

The article says the speeches were delivered in 349 BC and that Athens offered no military support; the entry dates them 349-348 BCE and says Athens sent limited aid. Neither the year of delivery nor the absence of aid is stated. The article's long 'Summaries' section is unsourced and partly contradicts the Content section; not used.

The article dates the proclamation of the Banat Republic to 31 October 1918; the entry has 1 November 1918. No date is given in the text. The entry says the republic was ended within weeks by Serbian troops; the article has Serbia occupying Timisoara in November but Roth formally deposed on 17 January 1919 (Maria Ormos: 20 February). The text speaks only of his own deposition. The Romanian release after a promise to stay out of politics is Brinzeu's account, also reported by Amerikai Magyar Nepszava.

The article dates his accession to c. 1483 after a three-year interregnum; the entry has c. 1480. The year is left out. The entry's brass manillas are not in the article. The article spells the epithet both n'Ibaromi and n'Ibarmoi; the first is used.
Rizzo Romano's claim that it was the first arms control pact left out (the entry says one of the earliest).

The entry speaks of two gunboats; the article of three French ships (the aviso Inconstant, the gunboat Comete and the mail steamer Jean Baptiste Say). The text names all three without a count. The entry says France blockaded the coast; the article says a blockade of the river. The text says only a blockade. Siamese naval strength that day is disputed between French accounts and Warington Smyth; left out.

The article dates the inauguration to 1256 Saka (1334) or 1258 Saka (1336); the entry has c. 1336. No year is given in the text. The Pararaton says the oath was fulfilled eleven years after he became mangkubumi, which does not fit the Bubat date of 1357 with either inauguration year; the eleven years are left out.

Article dates Prithviraj's raid on Mahoba to 1182-83 and the fall of Kalanjara to 1202 or 1203 (scholars disagree); the entry says 1182 and 1203. Disputed years left out of the text. Left out the ballads' detailed story (Udal, Malkhan, Brahmajit) as legend of doubtful historicity.
Article also lists the Boundary treaty of 1881 under this period, though it predates 1891: left out.
Article is short (about 350 words); the text keeps to what it gives.

The article is written largely from a Svetambara Jain point of view (Hindus 'encroached', 'attempts to destroy' Jain heritage) with thin sourcing; Jain claims are attributed to Jain tradition and the Ptolemy and Raja Gangasinh claims left out. The entry names Chauhan Rajput rulers and the year 1484; the article names the Patai Raval family and only 'the 15th century'. Neither the dynasty clash nor the year is stated in the text beyond what the article gives. Article gives the temple's height as 550 metres (1,523 feet), an inconsistent conversion: feet left out.
The article is about the state park; the text keeps to the prairie's history and setting.
The article gives Jawara becoming prime minister in October 1963 (History) and in 1962 (Notable members): year left out.
The article dates Streiff's original tune to the 1930s; the entry's dates say melodies of the late 1920s. Decade left out of the text.

The article gives the length as 48,700 lines, 48,686 couplets and the abridged version as 25,098 lines or couplets: these counts are inconsistent and are left out; the number of samut Thai books is given instead.

The entry says the soldiers killed 'many hundreds'; the article gives estimates of 'more than a thousand', '4,000 to 6,000' and '6,000'. No figure is given in the text; the entry's wording may need revising. Article is short; the text keeps to it.

SKIPPED: article is short (about 400 words) and confused: it says the Romans destroyed Pintia and buried the Vaccean culture, yet speaks of a Vacceo-Roman city and of Visigothic burials beside it; too little reliable material beyond the entry

The entry calls him a polo player; the article does not mention polo (no contradiction). Article dates the Tirah Campaign service to 1898 and an earlier service under General Ellis to 1897; years left out.
The article dates his reign c. 275–335; the entry c. 270–330. Reign years left out of the text.

The article says he was exiled to Turkey at the end of 1920 but also that he was arrested in Georgia on 13 October 1920 and went to France late in 1921; the text follows the dated sequence and does not date his arrival in Turkey.
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words, and the entry's description already holds nearly all of it

Diodorus's version has Pleminius die before his trial concluded; Livy has him put to death in 194 BCE after a failed escape plot. The text gives Livy's account, attributed, which agrees with the entry's date.

The article tells the arrival story and dates (1390, 1450, 1457) as fact, citing the Sulu genealogies; the entry treats Baguinda as a figure of Sulu tradition, so the text attributes them to the tradition. The article is short (about 450 words).
The article says Rosa was secretary general from 1876 to 1893, which conflicts with Soto's fall in 1883 and with the entry's 1876–1883; the end year is left out of the text.

The article dates the Golden Gate to Nepal Sambat 874 (1753 CE); the entry says 1754. Year left out of the text. The article names Kantipur and Yela as Bhaktapur's attackers; Yela is Lalitpur (Patan), named in the text as Lalitpur.

The article names the pirate father only as 'Thomas', possibly Thomas Tew, Thomas White or Thomas Collins (its lead says Tew); the entry says Thomas White. The surname is left out. The entry calls the mother 'a Malagasy princess'; the article calls Antavaratra Rahena a queen regnant. Her title is left out. The daughter is Bety in the entry, Bity in the article; her name is left out. The article says the federation lasted 'until 1750/51'; written as 'about the time of his death'.
The entry dates him only to the 12th century; the article gives 1113-1168, used here without contradiction.
The entry names the upheavals of 1672, 1747 and 1785 as dislodging the regents; the article lists more (1618, the deaths of William II and William III, 1787, 1795), told here as further examples.

The entry says the statute remained in force until 1915; the article says 'up till 1914'. The end date is left out. The article's claim that Ottoman troops had aided the attackers is unattributed; left out.
The article's comparisons with the cliff dwellings of Colorado and the church at La Jalca are left out.
The article gives the population both as 479,055 and (for 1901) 479,065; left out. The entry names Bombay State's merger year as 1948; the article gives no year, so none is given here.

The entry says he was killed 'probably in 1093'; the article gives 3 July 1093 without hedging. The day is left out. Some sources say the raiders were led by Gruffudd ap Cynan after escaping from Chester; left out as uncertain.
The article spells the uncle Gille Brigte (the entry Gilla Brigte); he is not named here. The article calls the wife both Helena and Elena de Moreville; Helena is used.
The referendum's year is not stated in the same sentence of the article; it follows the events of 1967, so only the day is given.
The article is short (about 290 words); the text keeps to what it gives.
The article says Timur 'might have had' camels loaded with burning kindling; hedged as 'is said to have'.
The article spells the martyr both Lalemant and Lalement; Gabriel Lalemant is used.

The article's claims of the first cinema in Central and South America and a population of 44,000 in the early 20th century are left out as doubtful; the entry speaks of silver mines, the article of gold and silver.
The article says the saint fled from 'Libia' (Libya); the place is left out as the spelling is uncertain.

The article gives the army's peak strength both as more than 80,000 active in 1990 and as 97,000; only the first is used. The article names the 1990s force both the SLA and EPS, and the 1995 successor as the National Army of Nicaragua or Nicaraguan Army; the entry's name and 1995 date are not repeated.

The entry says the church was completed in the early 18th century; the article gives only the building date 1720 and cornerstone of 12 September 1720. No completion date is given. The heritage-zone restrictions paragraph is left out as unsourced and promotional.

The article says the 1986 Sarbat Khalsa was also the occasion of a declaration of independence for Khalistan; left out as the article's statement is unexplained. The article calls the Mughal campaign after 1716 a genocide; described here by its measures.

The article says the larger temple is dedicated to Aniruddha (an avatar of Vishnu) and the smaller to Shiva, and that the larger was built for Mahipala's Vaishnava wife and the smaller for his Shaiva daughter-in-law; the entry says the pair is dedicated to Vishnu. Dedications left out. The article explains the name as 'mother-in-law and daughter-in-law' with no mention of Sahastrabahu, while the entry derives it from Sahastrabahu, a name of Vishnu. The etymology is left out.

The article dates the revivals under Jagjivan Das and Ghasidas to the mid-18th century in one place and Ghasidas to the 1820s elsewhere; the entry says the 1820s. Left undated except as the entry has it (not repeated). The article gives Jagjivan Das as 1670-1761? and elsewhere born 1682, and says he met Emperor Akbar, which cannot be right; Jagjivan Das left out of the longer text.

The article dates the attack with Dominique de Gourgue to 1567; the entry says 1568. Year left out. The article is about the chiefdom named after the chief; only what concerns him and his people's fortunes is used.

SKIPPED: article has about 250 words of substance and the entry already tells most of it (Greek mother, Olbia, Bacchic rites, execution by Octamasadas); only the flight to Sitalces, the exchange and the Niconium coins would be new
The article puts the stay near Victoria Falls in 1838 and also has Sebetwane striking north again around 1840; the entry dates the conquest of the Lozi around 1840. Both years left out.
The article gives Sechele's birth as 1812 without 'c.'; the entry has c. 1812. Birth year not repeated.

The article dates the coup and the start of the dynasty to 1469; the entry gives 1470. The year of the coup is left out. The article says Kanemaru set aside Shō Toku's family; the entry says he took the throne after Shō Toku's death. Worded without either detail.

The article says the inscriptions record two treaties in one place and one treaty elsewhere; the text speaks of the treaty and its curses without counting. The article's identification reads 'Ashurnerari V (Adad-nirari III or his son Tiglath-pileser III?)'; only the uncertainty is kept.
SKIPPED: article is mostly a quotation of Livy that the entry already summarises; beyond it only the etymology of the name and two sentences on historicity, under 250 words of new substance

The article gives his birth as 1869 in the lead and 1870 on his epitaph; birth year not repeated. The entry says the British made him president of the Busoga council in 1906; the article gives no year, so none is given.
The entry says the Senate survived under the last Sforza dukes; the article does not mention this. Not used.

The entry places the sealands between the Zuiderzee and the Weser; the article gives Alkmaar to Bremen in the myth, West Frisia to the Weser in the Treatise and West Frisia to Dithmarschen in the Gerda. Only the article's own formulations are used, none of them as a boundary of fact. The wp file ends at 'as follows:' without the list of sealands.

The article says the treaty was signed in 1682; the entry says 1682 or 1683. No year is given for the treaty itself, only Penn's arrival in late October 1682. The article is about the treaty; only what concerns the place and the treaty made there is used.
